decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has six short lessons. First, why sources are named at all. Second, what a reference needs and why one consistent style matters. Third, spotting and fixing citations that do not match your reference list. Fourth, identifying the sources in your own work and explaining why you acknowledged them. Fifth, why a source is logged the moment you select it, not afterwards. Sixth, keeping an organised source log as you gather evidence. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the six lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about referencing: naming your sources so a reader can judge your work and trace every claim back to where it came from. If you are starting out at university, this might be one of the first academic skills that feels unfamiliar. It is also one of the most practical: get it right from the beginning and you save yourself a great deal of trouble later.

By the end of this course you will be able to explain why sources are named, describe what a reference needs, spot and correct an inconsistent citation, identify and explain the sources in your own work, and build the habit of logging a source the moment you choose it, so your record stays organised and traceable.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Six flat learning outcomes, read from crs-07_tiered-outcomes (pathway-distillation profile: crs-03 is not-applicable), framed up front: naming sources, reference elements and consistent style, correcting inconsistent citations, explaining acknowledgement to a newcomer, logging a source at the point of selection, and keeping an organised source log.

practiceConnection.academic: Referencing is not an exam skill that disappears after this course. Every essay, report and dissertation you write from now on will ask you to name your sources accurately and consistently, and markers notice straight away when a reference list does not match what is cited in the text. Get the habit right now, while the stakes are low, and it becomes automatic long before it matters for a big piece of work.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Naming your sources, building a reference, and keeping everything in one consistent style are no longer unfamiliar: you now have a first, solid foundation in referencing. You can explain why sources are named, describe what a reference needs, spot and correct an inconsistent citation, identify and explain the sources in your own work, and keep an organised, traceable log of sources as you gather them. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: Start using what you've learned in the very next piece of work you submit: log each source as you choose it, check your reference list matches what you've cited in the text, and keep everything in one consistent style from the first draft. You will also use this habit of logging sources as you go when you come to finding and using sources for a longer piece of work.

decidedValue.whereNextBody: This is the first course in the Referencing pathway. The natural next step is the intermediate course, which moves from getting referencing right to judging it: checking a paraphrase against its source, weighing whether a reference list's range reflects real research, and handling source types that do not fit a standard template. The habit of logging a source as you select it, which you have just built, is exactly what makes that judgement possible later.
